I would like you to look at this paragraph with the title "Negative Experiences." Can you please look at that part of the document. Mr. Zilkic, you agreed with me that this event with 61 prisoners was a negative experience for your brigade, a very negative experience at that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And do you agree with me that that event involving the capture of 61 prisoners and this seizure is not even included as a negative experience of the members participating in the Farz operation; this only discusses booty and the preservation of material goods, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How can you explain the fact that this seizure is not even part of the report as a negative experience; what you are saying is that your brigade had 65 prisoners, actually, that is how you're presenting it?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can explain it only by saying that the mention of the 65 captured persons -- or, rather, that the El Mujahid was the bearer of assault actions and that as such, they considered them to be their own prisoners, that they took them away, they seized them from us, after which we reported this to our superior command, and we informed them about all the prisoners and said, amongst other things, that we had captured them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Zilkic, it says here that you -- your brigade captured these 65 people. It doesn't say that they were seized by the El Mujahid.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that several times the superior command was informed that the El Mujahid -- well, I cannot say now "seize," but the way we formulate it was that they had taken charge of or were handed over.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you say that in the analysis of the combat actions, which is a key document, if this is how it was, and that you had reported about that?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say why that was. I did not draft that document. The document was drafted by the staff. I cannot say why this was not said in that particular way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you signed the document, and you knew about the seizure of the 65 prisoners. The staff need not necessarily have known about it, but you knew about it.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the staff had to have known it as well, and I knew it too.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. Zilkic. Your Honours, I think this document already has a number, and perhaps it can be put away.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And about this, Mr. Zilkic, I would like to ask you the following: Actually, you and your brigade, in its composition, had the Asim Camdzic unit, which was not that different from the members of the El Mujahedin Detachment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand this assertion.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you will understand me more clearly after I show you a document. Could the witness see P2729, please. For the record, this is a document of the Military Security Service of the 35th Division of the 24th of October, 1995, and what is described here is the unit named "Asim Camdzic," and the document states -- can you please look at -- Your Honours, can we scroll down the document so that both in the English and the Bosnian we can see the bottom of this page. Okay, very well. And in the English version, we need to look at the following page, please. The Bosnian version, we need to look at the bottom of the page. So that we don't lose too much time and so that I don't have to read too much from the document, I would like to draw your attention to the part where it says: "They are quite independent ..." I am talking about the Asim Camdzic unit: "They are providing their own logistics and financial funds for themselves, all the captured war booty, the MTS vehicles, they are selling themselves and distributing the proceeds because of the basic assumption of its closeness and links to the El Mujahedin unit, the same from the last division of the war booty, gave each member 250DM each, and the commander of the 328th, Fuad Zilkic, is much respected by them and he commands and makes these agreements through the Commander Remzo Sinanovic or Huso Garandzic [phoen]." So Mr. Sinanovic was the commander of the Asim Camdzic unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that is a unit from your brigade, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that unit was very close to the El Mujahedin unit; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would in one thing. Members of this unit applied religious regulations 24 hours a day, and on that basis they were closer to the ideas of the El Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zilkic, do you recall at the end of your testimony I was asking you about other brigades of the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that not the 27th, the -- the 329th did not have these religious units in their midst?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And this unit, you will agree, the Asim Camdzic unit, from the beginning of its operation, was part of the units that were under your command?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I must say that by assuming my duties, I already found it in the establishment. It was already part of the establishment when I assumed my duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which duties?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duties of the Commander of the Municipal Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right, very well. And then you went to the 320th?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the Asim Camdzic unit also joined the 320th?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then to the 328th, and that unit also went to the 328th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all according to orders by superior commands. All right, very well. Now I would like --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Your Honours, can this document be given an exhibit number, and then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 810.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now look at P2377.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to talk about the situation in your 328th Brigade in general. We're talking about the 10th of August, 1995. Please, can you read the first segment here, if you can. If not, I'm going to quote. Can you please look -- well, you can see this first excerpt: "The latest events in the zone of responsibility ..."?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: " ... reflect a number of problems in the control of the 328th Brigade." And, Witness, would you agree that you actually had very serious problems in that brigade, that the situation in that brigade in this period was very serious?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I agree that the brigade was over-stretched that whole month, that it was exhausted, and that there was a series of factors that affected the control -- the system of control -- command and control.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can the witness now look at the last page of this document. We are talking about page 7 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at this last large document [as interpreted]. It gives an assessment of the situation in your brigade, and at some point -- it's the fourth line from the top. It says the main characteristic in the battalion is the fact that the RiK command-and-control system does not function at the level of the platoon commanders, the company commanders and also on the level of the battalion commands. The company commanders are rarely seen at the positions, and their coordination with the battalion commander is weak. And the question of numbers is something that is a burden. And I'm interested in the last sentence: "Disciplinary measures towards those who commit certain things are either not applied or not in accordance with the rules." Your Honours, that is on the following page of the English version. What I would like to ask you now, Witness, is this: Is it true that the organ of the 35th Division, the security organ, did carry out an inspection of your division?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that these reports were sent, but I also know that they never actually toured the lines of defence in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And is it correct, what it says here regarding the application of disciplinary measures towards perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. All those who violated rules were disciplined, and my security organ informed me that orders were issued that measures be applied.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your Honours, can this document be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 811.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like you to look at document P2403.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, would you agree -- can you look at this. This is a report -- or actually it's an act of the Command of the 35th Division of the 16th of August, 1995, and it's related to the elimination of weaknesses that were perceived. Can you please look at this introductory paragraph: "Pursuant to the order of the 3rd Corps Commander of the 10th of August, 1995, and with the aim of removing the weaknesses observed in the 328th BBR, the 35th Command hereby submits the following report on the measures undertaken and carried out so far." I just want to ask you: You know, surely, don't you, that the 3rd Corps Command ordered the application of measures in order to eliminate weaknesses in your brigade; you must know that, right?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what the order was, and I must say that all of these negative things were, conditionally speaking -- for example, the weakening of command and control was something that happened after the loss of 685 facility, and in fact after the capture of the newly-attained line, as of the 21st of July, 1995, I also reported to the Command that my brigade was not in a position to secure these lines itself, after which I was issued an order by the corps commander himself to keep the entire brigade on the lines throughout that whole month without any relief, replacements or anything like that, with the proviso that the lines achieved should be fortified.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, thank you. Your Honours, can this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say that this situation was the result of prior combat actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is meant by "685 facility"? Is that a specific elevation or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's a facility in the field, so it's an elevation that the El Mujahid captured in their actions. And since it was my task to take up and fortify the newly- achieved lines and to carry out decisive defence, after several days in an enemy attack, that facility was lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness, for that explanation. Can this document be given an exhibit number, Your Honours, please, and I would like the witness to look at another document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 812.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to look at Exhibit 596.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this document refers -- well, it's a document of the 35th Division, drafted on the 17th of August, 1995, and it talks about the combat readiness of the Command of units of the 35th Division. I would like you to look at the second paragraph. It talks about analysis of events in the area of responsibility of the 328th Division, precisely what you actually said just now about the fall of the lines, and it talks about, you will agree, that after the lines that were attained, the security organ has come to the conclusion that the RiK Command has totally failed, that the monitoring of the execution of measures and orders does not exist, very pronounced problems of false reporting, especially referring to the engagement of manpower in the brigades, non-existence of a line of control and command from the battalion command towards the company commanders and platoon commanders, and then they state the familiarity, abuse of positions, especially pronounced in the battalion commands, and so on and so forth. Please, do you agree that here it says that there is no control of the implementation of ordered measures and actions?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that for one simple reason. The stabilisation of the situation was something that I carried out with my superior officers, battalion and company commanders who were on the lines of defence around the clock. A lot of these things that are written down are not correct, they're not realistic. They did not tour the lines of defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Witness.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say this, too: After losing a part of the territory, my units set up new lines of defence by itself and held them for a month, until the next combat actions. This was something that could not have been achieved without the command-and-control system. There were many elements that had a negative effect, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down, slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I actually want to know about a single detail. How do you comment on this, pronounced problems of false reporting; what's your comment on that?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I refuse to comment on what they wrote or what they may or may not have meant. I don't know what they had in mind, but I do know that they were not familiar with the reality of the situation as it was on the ground. Saying this, that the command-and-control system was not functioning, well, somebody should go there and see for themselves, whether it was functioning and operating well or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you this: Do you agree that this is information that is being passed along the security line; right?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that your own security organ was involved in this?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So your brigade sends information on to the security organ of the 35th Division, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, an organ from your brigade, the security organ, is on the ground, right, you agree with that, together with you?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Now, Your Honours, could we please put this document away, and I would like the witness to look at 2522, P2522. My apologies, P2522.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zilkic, this is a document produced by your own brigade. It's an order, one would say, dated the 5th of September, 1995. Could we please see the signature. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Could we please see the top of the document. That is what matters, paragraph 1, item 1 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you see, Mr. Zilkic, this order is in reference to the Asim Camdzic unit, something we talked about a while ago, and the military police of the 328th Brigade. On the 5th of September, 1995, you issued an order for the Asim Camdzic unit and the military police of your brigade, in the area of responsibility of the 1st and 5th Battalions of the brigade, to withdraw back to base and to act upon any orders arriving from the commander, in other words, your orders; right?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So on the 5th of September, you pulled out the military police from the area covered by the 5th Battalion, which is where the incident took place, right, the Kesten area, Kesten village? That was their area of responsibility, was it not?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not from Kesten village. It could only have been from behind the lines where they were at the ready.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fine, fine, but you had command over that military police component, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This document is dated the 5th of September, but it orders that the action be completed by the 3rd of September. I'm looking at the English, if you could scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please just zoom in on the Bosnian. Your Honours, it says the pullout is to be completed, and what they mean is the units, by the 3rd. It's possible that there is something wrong about the date of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that a possibility, Witness, that you would accept? The date says "the 5th of September," and then it says "pull out by 1200 hours on the 3rd."

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it must be an error, right, concerning the date?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. What I find to be important is this: You had this military police unit under your control, the 328th Brigade; right? There was a military police unit under your command. How many?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A platoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is ...?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 30 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. My question now is this: At any point in time as that event was unfolding -- all right, sir. You were informed at one point this is what happened, some prisoners were seized, taken away, whatever. Did it ever occur to you to use that unit in this particular situation?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This unit was deployed as previously ordered by the Assistant Commander for Security of the 35th Division, in coordination -- actually, their assignment was defined and they were to work with the Military Police Company of the 35th Division. They were to serve as a protection unit. This was down the horizontal chain of command and control by the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, on the 5th of September, 1995, please, it reads: "Pull the unit out from the areas covered by the 1st and 5th Battalions, and continue to carry out any further assignments as ordered by the commander." And that's you?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the military police platoon was used. It was used in combat operations that were to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your Honours, can this document please be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 813.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please have Exhibit 586. These are rules governing the work of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How much longer are you still going to be, madam?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am drawing to a close. I will need, at the very most, about ten minutes more. I'll be very brief. Let's try to save some time, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you know what the rules are governing the work of the military police, don't you?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 6 displayed to the witness. This is page 5 in the English. Could we pull this down slightly so we can see the control part, "Control and command over military police."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it reads here: "Command and control of the military police is exercised by the commanding officer ..." Please go to the next page of the Bosnian. I think the English is fine. All right: "Command and control of the military police is exercised by the commanding officer of the military unit or institution to whose establishment structure the military police unit belongs or has been attached." You will agree with me, won't you, that you were the commander of a brigade in which an incident took place; you were the commanding officer of that brigade where this incident took place? Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, won't you, that this rule applied throughout the war, and it clearly says that you were in command of the military police unit of your brigade, you were in control of that unit; right?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In professional terms, it was the officer of the Military Security Service, and it was at his proposal that the unit was deployed and told to carry out a certain mission, protect units and territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite accurate. I see that you have got this fully worked out. Your Honours, both the witness and I were talking about paragraph 8, and I'm talking about the last sentence of paragraph 8: "A decision on the combat use of the military police unit is taken by the unit commander at the proposal of the competent senior military security service officer."

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, indeed, so, please, the situation is such that you are free to take a decision right away, if that is what the situation calls for, in order to have some sort of a solution, regardless of this proposal mentioned here. Secondly, you will agree with me that you had a security organ who at the time was, in fact, somewhere in the field; right?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that was because I sent them over to check what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Please, what I'm putting to you is this: It was your responsibility to immediately make use of that military police unit? I am putting that to you. Your responsibility was to straightaway make use of that military police unit in order to protect those people; if not, perhaps at least to try and see what was going on and what had become of those people. That is what I'm putting to you, Mr. Zilkic.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what you're putting to me, but if an entire battalion was unable to protect them, how do you expect that a military police platoon would have been able to accomplish that?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at least try to use it in that way, Mr. Zilkic?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had ordered the security organ to take whatever was in their power, whatever measures they could.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, right, I see. Can you tell us which precise security organ; first name, last name? Who?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I ordered directly to Enes Malicbegovic to go to provide any technical assistance to his own security organ on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fine, fine. That's your testimony, that's your evidence. Can you please just now look at D656. Did you ever ask Mr. Malicbegovic what he had found there?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you see, what we have before us right now is a document produced by the Intelligence Service of Republika Srpska. The date is the 8th of October, 2002. This is not a lengthy document. Could you please read it? I do wish to ask you a question or two about this. This is about information obtained by the Intelligence Service of Republika Srpska. Could we see the date in both the Bosnian and the English, the date for this report. So the date is the 8th of October, 2002. This document talks about information obtained by the Intelligence Service of Republika Srpska to the effect that at the so-called "12th Kilometre" there was a mass grave where members of the Army of Republika Srpska were buried who had been captured when the village of Vozuca was taken in Zavidovici Municipality at some point during 1995. The document goes on to say this, and I'm trying to save time, Witness. That's the purpose of this exercise: "The prisoners were taken in military trucks to the Zenica KPD." It also says that as they were passing through the village of Kucice, Zavidovici Municipality, they were intercepted and stopped by local Muslim extremists led by a man named Zilkic, and taken to the abandoned estate of Andrija Stankovic, where they were killed and buried in two mass graves. It goes on to state that a certain man named Edin Porobic used a dredging machine to dig up the bodies, after which he took them and buried them in a mass grave in the village of Gostovici. Then on the 8th of October, 2002, the bodies were still there. Mr. Zilkic, any comments?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first I hear of it, and I've certainly never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please pull this down a little.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You see that the document quotes three persons as sources. Mr. Zilkic, I'm telling you now that a grave was dug or dug up in this area, 2005 or 2006, I think, in the Gostovici area. It was what they normally called "a secondary grave." Any comments?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is I simply don't believe this to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is it that you can't believe?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That this is accurate information. First of all, I don't know who this "Zilkic" is who is referred to here. Secondly, I can't believe that Edin Porobic did anything of the kind. He wasn't born in 1964. This information is erroneous, it's random.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zilkic, you remember that at the beginning of my cross-examination, I asked you if there was another military commander in or around Zavidovici named "Zilkic"?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I said there was none.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So who could this be, this military commander, leader of the extremists, leader of people like Asim Camdzic?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are mere insinuations.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would object to the characterisation of "military commander." That doesn't at least appear in the English version. It talks about stopped by the local Muslim extremist led by a certain Zilkic. There's no reference in the English version, at least, to this Zilkic referred to in the document as being any kind of military commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Your Honours, I will tell you what the Bosnian says. "On the way through the village of Kucice, Zavidovici Municipality, they were intercepted and stopped by local Muslim extremists led by a man named 'Zilkic'." Your Honours, I didn't say "Commander Zilkic," I said "a man named Zilkic," but, okay, led by Zilkic, led by Zilkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, if you look at line 20 of --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I accept, I accept. I accept, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally cannot accept any of this. Firstly, Kucice, these could only have been refugees staying there. This is a village from which the Serbs had expelled everyone. Secondly, nobody would have taken anybody through Kucice on their way to the KP Dom in Zenica. Thirdly, whoever it was taken there had absolutely nothing whatsoever to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Zilkic, I hear you. Your Honours, can this document please be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution would object, Your Honour. There is no foundation based on this witness's testimony. In fact, the witness has explicitly repudiated and rejected what's contained in the document, and we would submit there is no proper foundation for this document to be admitted through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think there is a very good foundation for this, since there is reference here to the last name "Zilkic." The witness commented, and he did refute that. That much is true. But it still reads "Zilkic," it still reads "Muslim extremists," which is something that I've spoken of a lot, Asim Camdzic, that sort of thing. I talked to the witness about this. No matter whether the witness refused this or not, this is a document which I'm using to test the witness's credibility, Your Honour. And of course we can't expect a single witness to accept a document that is likely to challenge or question their credibility. This is a document testing the credibility of a certain witness, which in my opinion constitutes a more-than-sufficient foundation for this document to be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, if I may respond, Your Honour. Certainly, the witness was asked about the document. Madam Vidovic put extensive questions to the witness, she read parts of the document to the witness. That's certainly part of the record. The witness has answered the questions, and there's no independent basis for this document coming into evidence, there's no proper foundation. Certainly, he was asked about it. There are parts of the document that are now in the record in the form of those questions and answers, and the Prosecution would submit that there is no proper foundation for this document to come in through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is an exceptionally important document, in terms of the indictment, an exceptionally important document. As I said, it is being used to test a witness's credibility. The document also refers to an event, a development, that is very much the subject of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, if -- I mean, the document can't go in for two purposes, I would respectfully submit. If it's going in to challenge the witness's credibility, then that does not necessarily mean that it's going in for the truth of what's contained in the document. I'm also -- it's a bit unclear, at least from where I'm sitting or at this moment standing, how this document relates to an important core issue in this case. Without any more -- and I don't believe this witness is in a position to testify about that. I don't believe that this document necessarily goes to any core issue in this case. I mean, at one point we're talking about the document being tendered for the purpose of challenging the witness's credibility. On the other hand, it would appear as though my learned colleague is suggesting that the document might be relating to something else. And I don't think there's any proper foundation under either of those prongs for this document to come in at this time through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document has not been grounded, according to the Bench. There is no proper basis for linking it to this witness, and it cannot be admitted, therefor.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can it be marked for identification then, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document will then be marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI 814.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this brings my cross-examination to an end. I have no further questions, and I wish to thank you for the time that you have granted me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zilkic, Defence counsel showed you a document that was on the screen only for a short period of time, so I didn't quite have time to see the significance of it, but I would like you to have a look at that document again, and it is Exhibit 808, if the Registrar would be kind enough to put it up. I think it was supposed to be the duty shift log of the 328th Brigade. And it was on the page where -- and maybe Defence counsel can help me. It was on the page where there was a mentioning of one Chetnik soldier captured.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 5 of the Bosnian. Just a minute, Your Honour. Page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. There we are. It's on the duty shift on the 12th to 13th September 1995, and we are being informed that a Chetnik and one captured in the 4th sector point of convergence with the 2nd Corps, and that this man confessed that there were 40 well-armed Chetniks near the Borovci village and that they wanted to break out of encirclement. This obviously comes after the events that took place on the 11th of September, but my question to you is if the reference to these 40 well-armed Chetniks could be a reference to the group of Chetnik soldiers who actually were captured on the 11th of September.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It says here that a Chetnik was captured in a sector adjoining the other corps, which means the Kvrge sector. He was questioned and he said that in the surroundings of Borovci village, which had been taken in a previous attack, that we had passed them, that they had remained behind, and that they were now trying to break through from this encirclement, which means that they would have tried to break through our lines and link up with Ozren. So our deployment would be Kvrge 685 linked up with Podsjelovo. That's what the lines would have looked like on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sir, I'm unable to completely digest this piece of information, but, in any case, would you have any information about what happened to these 40 well-armed Chetniks later on? Were they able to break out or were they captured at a later point; do you know?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that at the place the 2nd and 3rd Corps met, there was a breakthrough by the enemy, some of their forces who had been lagging behind. It was exactly at the point of intersection between the two corps that a breakthrough occurred, and then the neighbouring Banovac Brigade suffered some losses from this, but I can't say anything more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What happened to the one Chetnik that you did capture and who you did interrogate and who did inform you about these 40 well-armed Chetniks? Was he handed over to the Mujahedin as well?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. I have another question which is of a more general nature, and that is -- that arises out of your testimony that you did not at any point meet personally with the El Mujahid Detachment leadership. Did I, understand this correctly?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I said that I met them three or four times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. I'm glad that you clarified this, because I was under the impression that you did not meet them. So you did meet them. And what were you told about the level of cooperation between the El Mujahid unit and your own troops?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I explained, at the first meeting, when I was called by the division commander, he said that this unit would be in my area of responsibility. That was the first meeting, where we were introduced to each other, and he told me about the command system of that unit. And he also said that through any orders by the division commander, it would have been my responsibility to make sure that they could stay in the area. Later on, it boiled down to logistic support, pursuant to orders by the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. It's an interpretation problem. I had not been following the interpretation, but I think there's a misinterpretation. Page 61, lines 11 and 20, the witness, and I heard this very clearly, said that he was familiarised with the command staff of the division, and the transcript reads "the command system of that unit," and he means the command staff of the El Mujahid unit, and this reads "system." So these are two entirely different matters, and I'm afraid that might mislead the Chamber. I think this is what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The best way to ascertain this is to ask the witness to confirm if, indeed, this is what you wanted to testify.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to say that he introduced me to the Command Staff, the Commander of the El Mujahid Detachment, Abu Maali. Muatez was in charge of combat activities, that's what I understood later, and there was an interpreter, too, named "Ajman."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Zilkic, I hope I'm not repeating questions that have already been put by the parties, but I do not have a clear idea of what your perception was of the distribution of command over the El Mujahid Detachment soldiers and your soldiers. In other words, were you supposed to exercise control over the El Mujahid Detachment forces?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that is entirely different unit, two entirely independent units. In both cases, the order was issued by the 35th Division, meaning I never received any orders from the El Mujahid Detachment, nor did I ever issue any orders to them, not in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So you were two units working together in parallel under the instructions of the 35th Division Command?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just two questions, sir. In answer to a question by Madam Vidovic, you said that you were coerced to make certain statements when you were making statements to the investigator of the OTP. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question is: Who coerced you?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not like that. It was the same as Mrs. Vidovic, who was trying to put me in a context where I would come across as an extremist, but she used documents for that purpose. It was in much the same way that the investigators did this. It was 10 or 12 years after the event. I had done my best to forget all about it, and then I was taken there to make a statement about something that I no longer remembered fully. They wanted certain answers to certain questions. If they didn't obtain their answers immediately, they would do the roundabout thing and then try to leave me in a spot where I could do little else but answer "yes" or "no" to certain questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, but they were not forcing you, anyway. Okay, thank you very much. The other question was: Again, in response to a question by Madam Vidovic, I think you said that your subordinate, from whom you say the El Mujahedin Detachment seized the POWs, informed you -- he phoned you, I think, twice, and the second time you said to him he must go back and try and get those POWs back or to go and find out what's happened to them; am I right? Now, my question is: Did he come back with an answer, and if so, what was the answer?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he told me right away that nothing can come of that, that they were taken away. Your Honour, I would like to repeat how the conversation proceeded. When he told me that there were prisoners, he asked for a vehicle to transport those prisoners, according to orders, to the place where prisoners were handed over. Immediately, I directed him to go to that spot where the people were arrested or captured, to the Kesten sector. After that, at about 1400 hours, he told me -- he called me to say that the El Mujahid had taken away the prisoners, had seized and taken the prisoners away. I asked him, "Can anything else be done without getting into a conflict with the Mujahirs," and he said, "No, it's too late, they've taken them away."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the short answer is: He didn't go back to go and check?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where he called me from the second time, but it was from that same sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but he did not pursue the POWs to try and get them back; is that what you are saying? It ended there, the matter ended on the telephone discussion?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZILKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me then that he couldn't do anything more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any questions arising?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We'd just like to thank the witness for appearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Thank you, sir. Then this brings us to the conclusion of your testimony, sir, and thank you very much for taking the time off to come and testify. You are now excused. You may stand down. Travel well back home. Sorry you had to stay the weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution calls Ferid Buljubasic, and he will be led by my colleague, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Yes, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir, and good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, could you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: My name is Ferid Buljubasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And could you please state your date of birth for the record?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 5th of November, 1953.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And could you please state your place of birth for the record again, sir?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: In Foca, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir. Sir, have you ever provided a written statement to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And do you recall when you were -- the date on which you were interviewed for the purposes of giving that statement?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: The first interview was on the 30th of July, if I remember correctly, and then on the 14th of August I signed the statement in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir. And at the time of that interview, sir, did you answer the questions that were put to you truthfully?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did you answer those questions freely, and that is, without any coercion?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And you've indicated that you signed the Bosnian -- excuse me, the English version of your statement on the 14th of August; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did you do that after the statement was read out to you in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would now ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P06208. If we could just scroll down a little bit on the English. If we could scroll down on it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, do you see your signature on the English version of the statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, in preparation for your testimony, you met with myself and an analyst from the Office of the Prosecutor, did you not?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And at that -- excuse me. At that point in time, you were given an opportunity to review the Bosnian language version of your written statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And after reviewing the Bosnian version of your statement, sir, were you given an opportunity to make corrections to your statement?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would now ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P06210.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you want us to do with P06208, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Again, the witness has made some corrections to this particular statement, so once he adopts the list of corrections, I would ask that this statement and the list of corrections be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. P06210.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, I object to this way of admitting statements. I believe that the Rule 92 ter is such that the witness would need to see and sign the statement, and I believe that he would need to see it and sign it in its Bosnian version. I really object for corrections to be admitted of a statement. This creates a lot of confusion. Instead of having a consolidated statement admitted, the corrections could have simply been entered and a corrected version could have been submitted, because last time we were in a situation where it was very difficult to see our way around such a statement. I object to this way, because then this uncorrected statement remains in the exhibits. You before have just now heard the witness speaking about bad translations and who objected to some things from the statement during the investigation phase. I think the statement would need to be given a provisional number, and then later it should be substituted by the consolidated statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would note that -- well, let me first add that the reason that this approach is being chosen is because there simply wasn't enough time to produce a consolidated written statement. I met with this witness on Sunday. I -- we produced the list of changes in Bosnian that day. That was immediately sent to the Defence on Sunday, itself. I simply did not have the language resources at my disposal to produce a consolidated statement by this afternoon. Had I had those resources at my disposal, I would have produced it, but there just wasn't enough time. I assumed that this particular practice would be okay, given that there weren't a substantial number of changes being made to the statement and given the fact that last week this particular practice was accepted with respect to another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand that you agree, in fact, that the correct procedure is to have a consolidated statement, and therefore you will file a consolidated statement in due course?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If -- well, let me say that's the ideal position, but I certainly think that the practice of submitting a list of changes, to the extent that that's presented in an ordered and concise manner, as it has been in this particular case, that should be sufficient. So I don't want the Court to understand my submission as being that that's the only way to present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fair enough. The Court then does order you to file a consolidated, corrected statement, okay, and offload this one that has got a correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. One -- just one submission that I'd like to make, Your Honour, that the -- it's -- the consolidated version of the statement is not going to be signed, unfortunately, because the witness will be leaving after his testimony and there won't be enough time to put his -- to get him to sign the statement before he leaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, there's a problem that's being raised.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that there won't be a problem, and I believe that the Prosecution will take into account the corrections given by the Prosecutor. We would accept for this to be done by the corrections on conditions that there aren't too many of them. But, Your Honours, please take a look. A large part of the statement has been corrected, and I did have a lot of difficulties in preparing for the cross-examination. We need to follow what is being said. I do not want that statements that were not signed by the witness, that he did not see in Bosnian and sign in Bosnian, should be admitted. I mean, we will accept a consolidated statement, although the witness did not sign with the paper where his signature is, but we will not accept this statement as it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. You will file a consolidated statement, signed or not signed, Mr. Menon, and in future let's try to have -- if there are corrections to be made, let's make a consolidated statement and offload the one that is incorrect and upload the one that is correct. And while I'm speaking, may I just ask, Mr. Menon, is there any specific reason that we were given the statement in triplicate, and it's so thick as a result, because every page is three times. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If I could have a moment to consult with my case manager, Your Honour. Am I to take it that Your Honour received three copies of the same statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no. I have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have three page 2s, three page 3s, three page what, three page what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, I apologise for that. There must have been a clerical error, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And we don't have the corrections that Madam Vidovic seems to be having.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I did actually forward that to the Defence and the Trial Chamber on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe it's our internal problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And then the signed version on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You may proceed, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. What I'll do is I'll just have the witness have a look at the corrections that he made and see if he's able to adopt those changes. I understand that the statement itself will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, does the document in front of you contain the changes that you wanted to make to your statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: I can see just one page. For now, this part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If we could just go to the next page. Perhaps if it would be quicker, I do have a Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, do you see this page?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Does this page list further changes that you wanted to make to your statement, sir? If we could go to the next page. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you see this page in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If we could go to the final page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, I'll ask you again, does the -- the document in front of you, does it contain the changes that you wanted to make to your statement?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And does your signature appear on the Bosnian version of the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, given the fact that we'll be submitting a consolidated statement, I don't really see any purpose in admitting this particular exhibit, other than just to note for the record that the witness did adopt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's just mark it for -- well, you can't mark it for identification. Given the problem that you raise, that the next statement will not be signed, I think it may perhaps just be prudent to keep this one on record so that we can compare the unsigned one with the signed one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So let's give this an exhibit number. Both of the two statements, give them an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And what Mr. Mundis just suggested to me is that this particular document be admitted into evidence, while the statement be marked for identification, and we'll substitute the consolidated statement for the list of changes, once we obtain it, if that's acceptable to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Keep both. Let them be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the statement will be Exhibit number 815, and the corrected version will be Exhibit number 816.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, if we could bring up Exhibit 815, which is the witness's statement. And if we could go to page 3 of the English and page 4 of the Bosnian version of the document. And if we could scroll down on the Bosnian version of the document. I want to focus on paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, do you see paragraph 8 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I want to focus your attention on the last sentence of paragraph 8. Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, when you made your corrections, did you change anything in respect of this particular sentence, the last sentence of paragraph 8?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: If this refers to the sentence: "If there was any written correspondence between the Administration and Rasim Delic, it went by our cabinet," I didn't change anything of that, but only in paragraph 8 I called the Administration by its proper name and added all the other administrations in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. I'm only interested in that last sentence, and what I want to ask you is whether there were ever any instances when correspondence from the administrations would reach General Delic without going through the Cabinet.

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: In the remainder of the statement, I said that the correspondence between the administrations and General Delic went through me. However, a part of this correspondence relating to the Administration for Personnel and Legal Affairs and some of the correspondence that was exchanged with the Security Administration went or bypassed me, or rather sometimes the chiefs of the administrations directly contacted General Delic so that a part of the correspondence did not go always via the Cabinet and through me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And do you know why this occurred, sir?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: That's also in the statement. It was probably due to the fact that we were in a hurry. It was necessary to sign some things urgently, and the Personnel and Legal Affairs Administration was in the same building, on the same floor, and it was close to General Delic's Cabinet, and probably because of this proximity and the frequent need for some acts and documents to be signed as soon as possible, the chief of the administration would take in the documents himself for review and for General Delic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did this also apply to the Security Administration, sir?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: From what I recall, very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we could -- if we could now move on to page 4 of the English and page 7 of the Bosnian version of the statement. And if we could scroll up a little bit on the Bosnian version of the statement. And if we could scroll a little bit down on the English version of the statement. I'm interested in paragraph 19, and all we see on the English version of the statement is a "9".

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, do you see -- do you see that in that paragraph, you refer to a reference number of a document that you were shown during your interview? Do you see that in paragraph 19?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would now ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P01983.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And is this -- if we could scroll up a little bit on the Bosnian version of the document. Is this the document that you were referring to in paragraph 19 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Possibly, in paragraph 19 and later in the amendments, I said that this was a document that was returned and that it had an envelope on which it said "To the commander personally" or to be opened by the commander. Based on this document, I cannot see whether that is that particular document. The documents were inside, so I don't see that this document states that the document should be opened by the commander. This is a copy of the document that has to be returned, but it doesn't say who should open it, it doesn't say what is stated on the envelope, and which I mentioned in paragraph 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, all I'm interested in is at paragraph 19 you refer to a type of document that would arrive in an envelope, and now the document that I'm showing you is called "a bulletin," and what I want to know is whether the document that you were referring to in paragraph 19 was a bulletin, not to the specific content of the document but just whether that document that you were referring to in paragraph 19 was a bulletin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. The witness has just said that the envelope was closed and he was not able to see, so you cannot insist any further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the document would come in a closed envelope. On the document, it said: "To be opened by the commander." Since I didn't open the document and I did not return it -- look at it once it was returned, it did not say that it was a bulletin on the envelope. Perhaps it was a bulletin, but I really cannot say what was in the envelope.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. Let's correct something, sir. The record says you said, "On the document, it said, 'To be opened by the commander.'" Now, were these words written on the document or were they written on the envelope? Is it the document that's to be opened by the commander or is it the envelope that's to be opened by the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander opens the envelope. He opens the envelope and -- maybe we can go back to paragraph 19 in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But just answer my question. The way it's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander opens the envelope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Listen to my question, please. Were the words "To be opened by the commander" written on the envelope or on something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the envelope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, I want you to listen to my question very carefully. I'm not asking you what you saw when you were the Chief of Cabinet, I'm asking you what you saw when you made this comment during the course of your interview. And what I want to know is whether, when making this comment during the course of your interview, you were looking at this particular document, because in paragraph 19 you refer -- you state: "I am shown document ERN-0403-7206" and I want to know, when you made that comment, were you referring to this particular document?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: If you read carefully paragraph 19, and I remember very well what I said there, this document, I did not see then when I was the Chief of Cabinet. I saw it in 2001, when I was performing the duty of deputy defence minister. Thus, the first time I saw this document was when it was shown to me when I was giving a statement. I saw it with you during proofing, and I am seeing it now. So I cannot say what was in the envelope, if on it it states to be opened by the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just listen to the question, sir. You're an adult person now. The question simply is: "On the 14th of August, 2007, when you made this statement, you said at paragraph 19, 'I am being shown --'" On the 14th of August: "I am being shown a document ERN-0403-7206. Is that -- is this the document that you were shown on the 14th of August, 2007, that you see in front of you, 0403-7206"? It's a very simple --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I simply wanted to note for the record that this document has already been admitted as Exhibit 727, and I simply wanted to illustrate what the witness was referring to when he made this comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please, but we should look at the witness's statement. He said: "I only saw such documents after the war."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not seeking to have this document admitted. I'm simply trying to identify it for the record so that when the Chamber looks at this witness's statement and they see the statement: "I am shown document ERN-0403-7206" Your Honours will know what the witness was talking about. That's all I'm doing this for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just don't understand what Madam Vidovic is saying, but, anyway, yeah, we understand that he saw it after the war, Madam Vidovic. In fact, we understand that he -- we're talking about things that he saw at the time he made the statement. You may proceed, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could go to page 6 of the English version of the witness's statement, which is Exhibit 815. And it's page 9 of the Bosnian version. If we could scroll down on the Bosnian version of the statement, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, it's the last sentence of paragraph 28, so we're going to have to move to the next page in the Bosnian version, but we'll stay on the same page in the English version. And, Your Honours, it's the fourth sentence of paragraph-- it's the -- let me count that. I believe it's the fifth sentence, actually. It begins: "The advantage of this meeting point ..." Can we go to the next page of the Bosnian version? Oh, we are. Thank you. Sir, have you had a chance to read that sentence?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: If you mean: "The advantage of this meeting point was the possibility of physical communication between Zenica," and then this was amended, it reads "Command Post Kakanj," is that what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one. I --

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: So this sentence was added to the statement in a supplement. It wasn't the forward command post, it was the command post of Kakanj, and something else was added. They most often met in Kakanj and Zenica for these very reasons, because there was the possibility of physical communication between Zenica and Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And what I want to know is what you mean by "the possibility of physical communication between Zenica and Kakanj." Can you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Sarajevo, as I believe you know, was under siege. You know what it took to leave Sarajevo, and you know how long it took to reach Kakanj or Zenica from Sarajevo. At the time when I was Chef de Cabinet, the BH Army controlled both Kakanj and Zenica. It was easy to communicate physically or, rather, to travel between Zenica and Kakanj. It was physically possible to reach Zenica from Kakanj, and vice versa, especially if you compared that to the communication between Sarajevo and either of these towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir. Now if we could go to -- if we could go to page 5 of the English and page 7 of the Bosnian version of this statement. If we could scroll up, and scroll a little bit down on the Bosnian version of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I'm interested in the fourth sentence of this paragraph, sir, paragraph 20, which says that -- a part of it reads Delic was often in Visoko as well. And what I want to know is how the communication -- how is the communication between Visoko and Kakanj, how is the state of communication between those two points?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Communication was possible between Visoko and Kakanj, and also it was a lot simpler, safer, than communication between Sarajevo and Visoko or between Sarajevo, Kakanj and Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you explain why it was simpler -- a lot simpler and a lot safer than communication between the other points that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: The road that one took at the time was also under the control of the army, and the distance between Visoko and Kakanj, which you can see on the map, is a lot shorter than that between Sarajevo and Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this not supposed to be a witness testifying pursuant to 92 ter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It is. I'm simply -- and that was the last point that I was going to have him clarify in his statement, but I identified a couple of points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why wasn't this clarified in the correction statements that you did on Sunday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The corrections that he made were -- on Sunday were his own corrections. I didn't want to input my own corrections into that or my own clarifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But then he's not giving -- now we've got to look at the statement and then look also at his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I apologise for that approach, Your Honour. My interpretation of Rule 92 ter was that -- was that we could ask clarifying questions. Another thing that I'd like to add is that on Sunday, I spent the whole day just compiling the changes that this particular witness wanted to add to his statement. I only actually started discussing the contents of his statement with him on Monday afternoon, and so there simply wasn't time to produce another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, there's the point, sir, that I guess you talk to your witness long in advance, not the day before, but, anyway, carry on. You said you had the last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: That was my last clarifying question on this statement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would now ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P02797.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, what does this document concern? And if you need to see more of the document, we can scroll down on it.

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: There is no need. If you look at the preamble, it's clear. It's about taking measures and incentives about the third anniversary of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in terms of awarding commendations and decorations to certain units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we see who produced this document? Do we see the witness's initials there? We need some link between the present witness and this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I understand the evidentiary rules that were issued by this Trial Chamber, it's not imperative that a document be admitted through the author of that document, and I was actually going to show the witness the person who signed the document and ask him about that, and then ask him a further question before I sought to tender the document. But I do think that the objection which was lodged was quite premature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you think you can then show him that signature and let him talk about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: That was my plan, Your Honour. If we could go to page 2 of the English and page 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Menon, I think you are used to showing the signatures later on. It might be good to show it beforehand, because that could save up some time, couldn't it? And that would also avoid objections being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I will keep that in mind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the document -- do you see the signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: To whom does that signature belong, sir?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: I've seen plenty of these, and this looks like General Delic's signature. I'm no handwriting expert myself. Therefore, I can't say with absolute certainty that the signature belongs to him. It certainly looks very much like the signature that he used whenever he signed documents that I submitted to him, but it would require the presence of a handwriting expert to ascertain that, especially in view of the fact that I did not author this document myself. It was the Administration for Personnel and Legal Matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, do you see the initials on the bottom left-hand side of the --
