utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, "AL SP/HC" with a check. This could be Alija Ismet and Salko Polimac, persons working in the personnel-related and legal issues at the time. "HC," I have no idea who that might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you explain the process by which an order such as this would have reached General Delic for his signature?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: This was an established procedure for all units when incentives were issued. Commanders and unit commanders, and we're talking about the 3rd Corps here, this is the Joint Command of the 3rd Corps, the Command of the 3rd Corps would forward this to the Administration for personnel-related and legal matters. They would prepare a document for these measures to be passed, and then the last thing would be for General Delic to sign this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I would ask this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I oppose this. Not through this witness, we don't have a sufficient foundation. The witness said this was a different administration that was behind this document. The signature is a little like it, but I don't even know -- this looks like "AL" to me. I don't think there is a foundation in relation to this witness, the same as the previous one, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Madam Vidovic. When you say, "The signature is a little like it," what do you mean? Are you testifying now or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no, no, no, Your Honour, I didn't say that. It must have been misinterpreted. I said the witness said that, that the witness said that it was like it, but he was no expert. And the other thing that I said, I see "AL" and not "AI."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's an error. I think this is Alija Lanca [phoen]. It's "AL."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would simply note that the witness said, "It certainly looks very much like the signature," and he also said,"I've seen plenty of these, and it looks very much like General Delic's signature." To me, he's identified the signature. That's a sufficient basis. I'm not going to add anything more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wasn't following the transcript, and I have to thank my colleague, Mr. Menon, for pointing this out, but that's not what the witness said, that it looked very much like it, and the way it was phrased, that wasn't what the witness said, that it was very much like it. He said it was like it, "but I'm no expert." I think this is something that can be clarified with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We can see the record here: "I've seen plenty of these, and this looks like General Delic's signature. I'm no handwriting expert myself, therefore I can't say with absolute certainty that the signature belongs to him. It certainly looks very much looks like the signature that he used whenever he signed documents that I submitted to him, but it would require the presence of a handwriting expert to ascertain that, especially in view of the fact that I did not author this document myself. It was the Administration for Personnel and Legal Matters." That's what's on the record. Do you confirm, sir, that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that there's not sufficient foundation for the tendering of the document. Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want it marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May it please be marked for identification and be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI 817.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may just ask, what happened to P01983?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was admitted previously through Witness Vuckovic as Exhibit number 727.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Part of the bulletin collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I noted that on the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, I just didn't write. Okay, fine, this is now 817. Thank you. This document is admitted into evidence. It is now given an Exhibit number 817. I beg your pardon, marked for identification. I'm so sorry. Yes, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: That concludes my direct examination, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Buljubasic.

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm Vasvija Vidovic. I will examine you on behalf of General Rasim Delic. You will have an opportunity to answer most of my questions with a simple "yes" or "no." This is the nature of cross-examination. We do encounter frequent problems with this, however. Please make a pause after each of my questions so that the interpreters can follow.

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Thank you for these instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In January 1995 -- from January 1995 to the end of the war, you were Chef de Cabinet of the General Staff commander; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were preceded by Mr. Murat Softic in this position; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of your statement you describe the personnel composition of the commander's cabinet. You said that there were two secretaries working there and a typist. One of those was Jasna Lemes; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I amended paragraph 3. There was a person who made coffee for us, and I provided the names of the persons who were secretaries, Haris Huselimovic and Jasna Lemes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Zeljko Grubesic was there too; right? He was in charge of liaising with the media?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned the bodyguards, too, Mr. Dedic and Mr. Akova. They were there throughout; right? You mentioned the bodyguards, right, Mr. Dedic and Mr. Akova; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: D-E-D-I-C and A-K-O-V-A, Dedic and Akova. They were always with General Delic whenever he travelled; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know, but at one point I left -- or, rather, when they left Sarajevo, I don't know if they both went with him, but every time General Delic left Sarajevo, both of them were with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said something about the Kakanj command post a while ago, or you said it in your statement, that it reads this was, in a way, a new meeting point, a new place for meetings. Was this, in actual fact, the Kakanj command post? It was a command post of the BH Army Staff, was it not?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't remember saying anywhere in my statement that this was a new meeting point, a meeting place. I did say that meetings were held there and in corps commands because of Sarajevo's physical isolation. It's not that this was some sort of a special place where meetings were held.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that explanation. You did not go to Kakanj yourself. In your statement, you say that you went there no more than twice; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The reason being General Delic didn't spend that much time in Kakanj, he didn't spend that much time working there; he would mostly just pass through, stay very briefly, and the Chef de Cabinet's presence was not required, was it?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: What I said was that General Delic sometimes left Sarajevo for Kakanj when he was on his way to tour the units, when he was on his way to tour the main Logistics Centre in Visoko, or when he was on his way out of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I really don't know how long or when he stayed in any of these places. I knew about when he travelled abroad. I would know the duration of most of those trips, in rough terms. Therefore, I can't say whether it was long, short. I have no documents to indicate this. I wasn't always aware of whether he was in Kakanj, in Visoko, touring the units, somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. At any rate, in Kakanj he used an office, but he didn't really have his own office, such as prescribed by the rules governing the work of the Supreme Command Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: There is an addendum to the statement, and that is precisely what is stated there. General Delic, during his time in Kakanj, would use a room belonging to the Staff. He would have one of the people from the Army Staff in Kakanj catering to his needs. Occasionally, Jasna Lemes, the secretary, would travel along with him, and it's all in the addendum to my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would you agree that General Delic's work, for the most part, was done in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: I can confirm that for as long as I was Chef de Cabinet, he spent the best of his time in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. All these questions that I'm asking you, just for you to know, is mostly to do with your time as Chef de Cabinet. I'm talking about 1995. We have a minute or two left, and I will ask you one or two questions about his purview, the scope of his work in Sarajevo, and this is something that concerned you. His tasks and your tasks were also to liaise with the Supreme Command, of which he himself was a member; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This required the presence of General Delic at meetings of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: His activities were directly linked to the work of the Government and the Defence Ministry as a governed body; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Contacts with the Defence Ministry, which was based in Sarajevo, were frequent and important as well, were they not?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Indeed, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He worked in Sarajevo, and he also maintained relations with UNPROFOR; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, UNPROFOR and all the other international players who were in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed. A lot of other international organisations who were in Sarajevo at the time?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And there were many of those at the time, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe this is a good time to stop my cross-examination for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. We unfortunately are not -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I just wanted to add one thing so that the record is clear. Once we get the consolidated statement, what we'll do is we'll add it to Exhibit 816, which is the changes which Mr. Buljubasic has signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine, just liaise with the Court Registrar and you can advise us what has happened. Unfortunately, we haven't finished with you, sir. You'll have to come back tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. Okay? Court adjourned to quarter past 2.00 tomorrow afternoon in the same court. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 14th day of September, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.
